docs.title: VFS - Virtual Filesystem CLI
docs.text: A command-line tool that implements a fully-featured virtual filesystem backed by embedded databases. Manage files, directories, and content using familiar shell commands without touching the real filesystem.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• :material-folder-multiple: Familiar Commands Use ls, cp, mv, rm, cat, mkdir, and more

  • :material-database: Pluggable Storage SQLite (default), Sled, LMDB, or RocksDB backends

  • :material-safe-square: Multiple Vaults Create and switch between independent databases

  • :material-history: Version History Automatic versioning on every file change with rollback support

  • :material-tag-multiple: Metadata & Tags Add custom tags and metadata to any file

  • :material-magnify: Full-Text Search Fast content search (FTS5 for SQLite, Tantivy for others)

  • :material-regex: Grep Support Regex-based content searching across files

  • :material-console: External Commands Run bash commands on virtual files via exec or pipes

  • :material-console-line: Interactive Shell REPL mode where you don't need to prefix commands with vfs

  • :material-robot: Agent-Friendly JSON output, snapshots, quotas, and audit logs for AI agent integration

  • :material-harddisk: FUSE Mount Mount vaults as real directories (Linux/macOS)

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
# Create a new vault
vfs vault create myproject

# Create directories and files
vfs mkdir /docs
vfs write /docs/readme.txt "Hello, World!"

# List files
vfs ls /docs

# Read file contents
vfs cat /docs/readme.txt

# Search for content
vfs grep "Hello" /docs/

# View version history
vfs log /docs/readme.txt

# Enter interactive shell
vfs shell

docs.title: Agent Integration
docs.text: This guide explains how to use VFS as a sandboxed filesystem for AI agents.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
VFS provides a safe, isolated filesystem for AI agents to:

  • Read and write files without touching the real filesystem
  • Experiment freely with snapshot/restore for rollback
  • Operate within resource quotas to prevent runaway behavior
  • Debug issues via audit logs

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import subprocess
import json

class VFS:
    def __init__(self, vault="agent-workspace"):
        self.vault = vault

    def run(self, *args):
        """Execute a vfs command and return parsed JSON."""
        cmd = ["vfs", "--vault", self.vault, "--json"] + list(args)
        result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode != 0:
            error = json.loads(result.stdout) if result.stdout else {"error": result.stderr}
            raise Exception(f"vfs error: {error}")
        return json.loads(result.stdout) if result.stdout else None

# Initialize
vfs = VFS("agent-workspace")

# Create workspace
vfs.run("mkdir", "/workspace")
vfs.run("write", "/workspace/hello.txt", "Hello, World!")

# Read back
result = vfs.run("cat", "/workspace/hello.txt")
print(result["content"])  # "Hello, World!"

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text: Snapshots save the entire vault state, allowing agents to experiment and rollback.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
# Save state before experiment
$ vfs snapshot save before-experiment

# Agent does work...
$ vfs mkdir /experiment
$ vfs write /experiment/code.py "print('test')"
$ vfs rm /important/file.txt  # Oops!

# Restore to saved state
$ vfs snapshot restore before-experiment

# /important/file.txt is back, /experiment is gone

docs.title: Snapshot Commands
docs.text:

vfs snapshot list

# Save with description
vfs snapshot save checkpoint-1 -d "Before refactoring"

# Get snapshot info
vfs snapshot info checkpoint-1

# Delete a snapshot
vfs snapshot delete checkpoint-1

docs.title: Agent Pattern: Experiment Loop
docs.text:
def experiment_safely(vfs, experiment_fn):
    """Run experiment with automatic rollback on failure."""
    # Save state
    snapshot = vfs.run("snapshot", "save")
    snapshot_name = snapshot["name"]

    try:
        result = experiment_fn()
        return {"success": True, "result": result}
    except Exception as e:
        # Rollback on failure
        vfs.run("snapshot", "restore", snapshot_name)
        return {"success": False, "error": str(e), "rolled_back": True}
    finally:
        # Clean up snapshot
        vfs.run("snapshot", "delete", snapshot_name)

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text: Quotas prevent agents from consuming excessive resources.

docs.title: Setting Quotas
docs.text:
# Set limits
vfs quota set max_size_mb 100       # Total vault size
vfs quota set max_files 10000       # Maximum file count
vfs quota set max_file_size_mb 10   # Single file limit

# View current limits
vfs quota

docs.title: Quota Errors
docs.text:
When quotas are exceeded, operations fail with clear errors:

{
  "error": "QuotaExceeded",
  "message": "File size (15 MB) exceeds max_file_size_mb (10 MB)",
  "type": "max_file_size_mb",
  "requested": 15,
  "limit": 10
}

docs.title: Agent Pattern: Check Before Write
docs.text:
def safe_write(vfs, path, content):
    """Write with quota awareness."""
    info = vfs.run("stats")

    content_size_mb = len(content.encode()) / (1024 * 1024)

    # Check against limits before writing
    if content_size_mb > 10:  # max_file_size_mb
        raise Exception(f"Content too large: {content_size_mb:.1f}MB")

    return vfs.run("write", path, content)

docs.title: Complete Agent Example
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example agent harness using vfs."""

import subprocess
import json

class VFSAgent:
    def __init__(self, vault_name="agent-workspace"):
        self.vault = vault_name

    def run(self, *args):
        """Execute vfs command, return parsed JSON."""
        cmd = ["vfs", "--vault", self.vault, "--json"] + [str(a) for a in args]
        result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)

        if result.stdout:
            data = json.loads(result.stdout)
            if result.returncode != 0:
                raise Exception(f"VFS Error: {data.get('message', data)}")
            return data
        return None

    def checkpoint(self, name=None):
        """Save current state."""
        args = ["snapshot", "save"]
        if name:
            args.append(name)
        return self.run(*args)

    def rollback(self, name):
        """Restore to checkpoint."""
        return self.run("snapshot", "restore", name)

    def read(self, path):
        """Read file contents."""
        result = self.run("cat", path)
        return result["content"]

    def write(self, path, content):
        """Write file contents."""
        return self.run("write", path, content)

    def ls(self, path="/"):
        """List directory."""
        result = self.run("ls", path)
        return result["entries"]

    def mkdir(self, path):
        """Create directory."""
        return self.run("mkdir", "-p", path)

    def rm(self, path, recursive=False):
        """Remove file or directory."""
        args = ["rm"]
        if recursive:
            args.append("-r")
        args.append(path)
        return self.run(*args)

# Usage
agent = VFSAgent("demo-agent")
agent.mkdir("/project/src")
agent.write("/project/src/main.py", "print('Hello!')")

def cleanup_old_snapshots(agent, keep=5):
    snapshots = agent.run("snapshot", "list")["snapshots"]
    snapshots.sort(key=lambda s: s["created"])
    for snap in snapshots[:-keep]:
        agent.run("snapshot", "delete", snap["name"])

docs.title: FUSE Mount
docs.text:
VFS can mount a vault as a real directory using FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace), enabling use of standard tools like ls, cat, vim, and others on virtual files.

Feature Flag Required

FUSE support requires building with the fuse feature and installing libfuse3.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install libfuse3-dev

# Fedora
sudo dnf install fuse3-devel

# Arch
sudo pacman -S fuse3

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: brew install macfuse

docs.title: Build with FUSE Support
docs.text: cargo build --release --features fuse

docs.title: Basic Mount
docs.text:
# Create mount point
mkdir -p /tmp/vfs-mount

# Mount vault
vfs mount <vault-name> <mountpoint> --foreground

Example:

$ vfs mount myproject /tmp/vfs-mount --foreground
Mounting myproject at /tmp/vfs-mount (foreground mode)
Press Ctrl+C to unmount

docs.title: Mount Options
docs.text:
Option Description --foreground Run in foreground (for debugging) --readonly Mount read-only --allow-other Allow other users to access

Examples:

# Read-only mount
vfs mount myproject /tmp/vfs-mount --foreground --readonly

# Allow other users (requires /etc/fuse.conf configuration)
vfs mount myproject /tmp/vfs-mount --foreground --allow-other

docs.title: Using the Mount
docs.text: Once mounted, use standard Unix tools:

docs.title: List Files
docs.text: ls -la /tmp/vfs-mount/

docs.title: Read Files
docs.text:
cat /tmp/vfs-mount/docs/readme.txt
less /tmp/vfs-mount/docs/readme.txt

docs.title: Write Files
docs.text: echo "New content" > /tmp/vfs-mount/newfile.txt

docs.title: Edit with Editors
docs.text:
vim /tmp/vfs-mount/docs/readme.txt
nano /tmp/vfs-mount/config.yaml
code /tmp/vfs-mount/  # VS Code

docs.title: Create Directories
docs.text:
mkdir /tmp/vfs-mount/newdir
mkdir -p /tmp/vfs-mount/path/to/nested

docs.title: Copy and Move
docs.text:
cp /tmp/vfs-mount/file.txt /tmp/vfs-mount/backup.txt
mv /tmp/vfs-mount/old.txt /tmp/vfs-mount/new.txt

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
rm /tmp/vfs-mount/unwanted.txt
rm -r /tmp/vfs-mount/old-directory/

docs.title: Using vfs unmount
docs.text: vfs unmount /tmp/vfs-mount

docs.title: Using fusermount
docs.text:
fusermount -u /tmp/vfs-mount

# Lazy unmount (if busy)
fusermount -uz /tmp/vfs-mount

docs.title: Ctrl+C (Foreground Mode)
docs.text: If running in foreground mode, press Ctrl+C to unmount.

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
Changes made through the FUSE mount are immediately visible via VFS commands:

# Create file via FUSE
echo "Hello" > /tmp/vfs-mount/hello.txt

# Verify via VFS command
vfs --vault myproject cat /hello.txt
# Output: Hello

And vice versa:

# Create file via VFS
vfs --vault myproject write /world.txt "World"

# Read via FUSE
cat /tmp/vfs-mount/world.txt
# Output: World

docs.title: Version History
docs.text:
Writes through FUSE create new versions just like VFS commands:

# Write multiple times
echo "Version 1" > /tmp/vfs-mount/file.txt
echo "Version 2" > /tmp/vfs-mount/file.txt
echo "Version 3" > /tmp/vfs-mount/file.txt

# Check version history
vfs --vault myproject log /file.txt

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. No symlinks: VFS doesn't support symbolic links
  2. No hard links: Not supported
  3. No extended attributes: Use vfs meta instead
  4. Single user: No multi-user permission model
  5. No concurrent mount: Don't mount the same vault twice

docs.title: IDE Integration
docs.text:
Mount a vault and open in your IDE:

vfs mount myproject ~/vfs-project --foreground &
code ~/vfs-project

docs.title: Backup Tools
docs.text:
Use standard backup tools on virtual files:

vfs mount myproject /tmp/mount --foreground --readonly &
rsync -av /tmp/mount/ /backup/destination/

docs.title: Shell Scripts
docs.text:
Process virtual files with shell scripts:

vfs mount myproject /tmp/mount --foreground &
for f in /tmp/mount/data/*.csv; do
    process_csv "$f"
done
vfs unmount /tmp/mount

docs.title: Permission Denied
docs.text:
fusermount: user has no write access to mountpoint

Ensure you have write permission to the mount directory:

mkdir -p /tmp/vfs-mount
chmod 755 /tmp/vfs-mount

docs.title: Transport Endpoint Not Connected
docs.text:
ls: cannot access '/tmp/vfs-mount': Transport endpoint is not connected

The mount crashed or was improperly terminated. Force unmount:

fusermount -uz /tmp/vfs-mount

docs.title: FUSE Not Available
docs.text:
fuse: device not found

Load the FUSE kernel module:

sudo modprobe fuse

docs.title: allow_other Error
docs.text:
fusermount3: option allow_other only allowed if 'user_allow_other' is set in /etc/fuse.conf

Edit /etc/fuse.conf and uncomment user_allow_other, or don't use --allow-other.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text: VFS provides tools to manage vault size and performance through pruning old versions, garbage collection, and database compaction.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Over time, vaults accumulate:

  • Old file versions
  • Orphaned content blobs (unreferenced data)
  • Database fragmentation

Regular maintenance keeps vaults performant and storage-efficient.

docs.title: Keep N Versions
docs.text:
Retain only the last N versions of each file:

vfs prune --keep <N>

Example:

$ vfs prune --keep 5
Pruning versions, keeping last 5 per file...
Removed 1,234 old versions
Freed 45.2 MB (run 'vfs compact' to reclaim space)

docs.title: Time-Based Pruning
docs.text:
Remove versions older than N days:

vfs prune --older-than <DAYS>

Example:

$ vfs prune --older-than 30
Pruning versions older than 30 days...
Removed 892 old versions
Freed 23.1 MB

docs.title: Combined Strategies
docs.text:
Strategies can be combined:

# Keep last 10 versions AND remove anything older than 90 days
vfs prune --keep 10 --older-than 90

docs.title: Prune Specific Files
docs.text:
Target specific files or patterns:

vfs prune --keep 3 /logs/*.log
vfs prune --older-than 7 /cache/

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Preview what would be pruned without actually deleting:

$ vfs prune --keep 5 --dry-run
DRY RUN - No changes will be made

Would remove:
  /docs/readme.txt: 12 versions (keeping 5)
  /src/main.rs: 8 versions (keeping 5)
  ...

Total: 1,234 versions, 45.2 MB

docs.title: Garbage Collection
docs.text: Garbage collection removes orphaned content blobs - data that's no longer referenced by any file or version.

docs.title: When Orphans Occur
docs.text:
Content becomes orphaned when:

  • All versions referencing it are pruned
  • Files are deleted
  • Content is replaced

docs.title: Run GC
docs.text:
vfs gc

Example:

$ vfs gc
Scanning for orphaned content...
Found 234 orphaned blobs (12.5 MB)
Removing orphaned content...
Done. Run 'vfs compact' to reclaim disk space.

docs.title: Compaction
docs.text:
After pruning and GC, the database file still occupies the same disk space. Compaction reclaims unused space.

vfs compact

Example:

$ vfs compact
Compacting vault 'myproject'...
Before: 125.3 MB
After: 89.7 MB
Freed: 35.6 MB

docs.title: What Compact Does
docs.text:
1. Runs garbage collection (if not recently run)
  2. Rebuilds FTS index
  3. Executes SQLite VACUUM
  4. Optimizes indexes

docs.title: Full Maintenance Routine
docs.text:
Complete maintenance in one command:

vfs maintain

This runs:

  1. Prune (using vault's configured strategy)
  2. Garbage collection
  3. Compaction
  4. Index optimization

Example:

$ vfs maintain
Starting maintenance for vault 'myproject'...

[1/4] Pruning old versions...
      Removed 456 versions

[2/4] Garbage collection...
      Removed 123 orphaned blobs

[3/4] Compacting database...
      Freed 28.4 MB

[4/4] Optimizing indexes...
      Done

Maintenance complete.
Before: 156.2 MB
After: 127.8 MB

docs.title: Vault Statistics
docs.text:
vfs stats

Shows:

  • Total size
  • File count
  • Version count
  • Content blob count

docs.title: Storage Breakdown
docs.text:
$ vfs stats
Storage Breakdown:
  Content blobs:  89.2 MB (1,234 blobs)
  Version data:   12.3 MB (5,678 versions)
  Metadata:       2.1 MB
  FTS index:      8.5 MB
  ──────────────────────
  Total:          115.3 MB

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Regular maintenance: Run vfs maintain weekly for active vaults
  2. Dry run first: Always preview with --dry-run before pruning
  3. Backup before major cleanup: Export important files before aggressive pruning
  4. Compact after bulk operations: Always compact after large imports/deletes

docs.title: Vault Size Not Decreasing
docs.text:
After pruning/GC, run compact:

vfs compact

If size still doesn't decrease, check for:

  • Large remaining files: vfs find / --min-size 10485760
  • Files with many versions: vfs stats

docs.title: Slow Pruning
docs.text:
For large vaults, prune in batches by directory:

for dir in /docs /src /data; do
    vfs prune --keep 5 "$dir"
done

docs.title: Recover from Aggressive Pruning
docs.text:
If you pruned too aggressively:

  • Check for backups
  • Recent changes may still be in SQLite WAL

Prevention: Always use --dry-run first.

docs.title: Storage Backends
docs.text: VFS uses a pluggable storage backend architecture, allowing different embedded databases to be used as the underlying storage engine.

docs.title: Available Backends
docs.text: Backend Best For Trade-offs SQLite (default) General use, queries Larger files, slower writes Sled High write throughput No SQL, newer LMDB Read-heavy, memory-mapped Fixed map size RocksDB Large datasets, LSM More dependencies

docs.title: SQLite (Default)
docs.text:
The default backend using SQLite with FTS5 for full-text search.

Pros:

  • Battle-tested, widely used
  • Built-in FTS5 for search
  • SQL queries for debugging
  • Single-file database
  • Good tooling (DB Browser, etc.)

Cons:

  • Write amplification for small updates
  • Larger file size overhead
  • Global write lock

Usage:

vfs vault create myproject --backend sqlite

docs.title: Sled
docs.text:
A modern embedded database written in Rust, using a Bw-tree architecture.

Pros:

  • Pure Rust, no C dependencies
  • High write throughput
  • Lock-free reads
  • Built-in compression

Cons:

  • No SQL queries
  • Requires separate search index (tantivy)
  • Younger project

Usage:

vfs vault create myproject --backend sled

docs.title: LMDB
docs.text:
Lightning Memory-Mapped Database - extremely fast reads via memory mapping.

Pros:

  • Very fast reads
  • Memory-mapped for efficiency
  • Proven in production (OpenLDAP)
  • ACID compliant

Cons:

  • Fixed maximum database size
  • Write-heavy workloads less efficient
  • Requires separate search index

Usage:

vfs vault create myproject --backend lmdb

docs.title: RocksDB
docs.text:
LSM-tree based storage engine from Facebook, designed for SSDs.

Pros:

  • Excellent for large datasets
  • Good write performance
  • Compression tiers
  • Column families

Cons:

  • Large binary dependency
  • Complex tuning
  • More resource usage

Usage:

vfs vault create myproject --backend rocksdb

docs.title: At Vault Creation
docs.text:
# Explicit backend selection
vfs vault create myproject --backend sled

# Use default (SQLite)
vfs vault create myproject

docs.title: Choosing Based on Workload
docs.text: Workload Recommended Backend General purpose SQLite Write-heavy (logs, imports) Sled or RocksDB Read-heavy (serving) LMDB Large datasets (>10GB) RocksDB Maximum compatibility SQLite Minimal dependencies Sled

docs.title: Search Implementations
docs.text: Storage Backend Search Implementation SQLite FTS5 (built-in) Sled Tantivy LMDB Tantivy RocksDB Tantivy

docs.title: Migration Between Backends
docs.text:
Convert a vault from one backend to another:

vfs vault migrate myproject --to sled

This:

  1. Creates a new vault with the target backend
  2. Copies all data (files, versions, tags, metadata)
  3. Verifies integrity
  4. Optionally removes the old vault

docs.title: Migration Options
docs.text:
# Keep original vault
vfs vault migrate myproject --to sled --keep-original

# Custom destination
vfs vault migrate myproject --to lmdb --output /path/to/new.vfs

# Verify without migrating
vfs vault migrate myproject --to sled --dry-run

docs.title: Backend Not Available
docs.text:
Error: Backend 'rocksdb' is not compiled in this build

VFS may be compiled without certain backends. Check available backends:

vfs --version

docs.title: Migration Fails
docs.text:
Try manual migration:

# Export all data
vfs export / /tmp/vault-export --recursive

# Create new vault with desired backend
vfs vault create newvault --backend sled

# Import data
vfs --vault newvault import /tmp/vault-export /

docs.title: Performance Issues
docs.text:
Check backend statistics:

vfs stats

Try compaction:

vfs compact

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Understanding these concepts will help you get the most out of VFS.

docs.title: Vaults
docs.text:
A vault is a self-contained virtual filesystem stored in a single database file.

~/.vfs/
├── project-a.vfs    # One vault
├── project-b.vfs    # Another vault
└── experiments.vfs  # A third vault

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• Isolated: Each vault is completely independent
  • Portable: Copy the .vfs file to move your entire filesystem
  • Single File: Everything (files, directories, metadata, versions) in one file

docs.title: Working with Vaults
docs.text:
# Create a vault
vfs vault create myproject

# List vaults (current marked with *)
vfs vault list

# Switch vaults
vfs vault use another-project

# Use a specific vault for one command
vfs --vault myproject ls /

docs.title: Content-Addressable Storage
docs.text:
VFS uses content-addressable storage (CAS), where files are stored by the SHA-256 hash of their content.

                    ┌─────────────────┐
    file-a.txt ───▶ │  sha256: abc123 │
                    │  "Hello World"  │
    file-b.txt ───▶ │                 │ ◀─── Same content,
                    └─────────────────┘      stored once!

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
1. Automatic Deduplication: Identical content is stored only once
  2. Efficient Versioning: New versions only store changed content
  3. Integrity: Content is verified by hash on every read
  4. Space Savings: Multiple files pointing to same content share storage

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Create two files with identical content
vfs write /file1.txt "Hello World"
vfs write /file2.txt "Hello World"

# Check storage - only one blob exists!
vfs stats
# Blobs: 1, Total size: 11 bytes

docs.title: Automatic Versioning
docs.text:
Every modification to a file creates a new version. VFS keeps the complete history.

/docs/readme.txt
├── Version 1: "Initial content"     (created)
├── Version 2: "Updated content"     (modified)
├── Version 3: "Fixed typo"          (modified)
└── Version 4: "Final version"       (current)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Write Operation: Creates new version, old versions preserved
  2. Version Storage: Each version points to a content blob (via SHA-256)
  3. No Deltas: Full content stored (but deduplicated via CAS)

docs.title: Working with Versions
docs.text:
# View history
vfs log /docs/readme.txt

# Read specific version
vfs cat -v 2 /docs/readme.txt

# Compare versions
vfs diff /docs/readme.txt --v1 1 --v2 3

# Restore old version (creates new version with old content)
vfs checkout /docs/readme.txt -v 2

docs.title: File Entry Contains
docs.text:
• Path and name
  • Type (file or directory)
  • Size
  • Timestamps (created, modified)
  • Version number
  • Reference to content blob
  • Parent directory reference

docs.title: Content Blob Contains
docs.text:
• Raw file content
  • Identified by SHA-256 hash
  • Shared across files/versions with same content

docs.title: Tags and Metadata
docs.text: VFS supports rich metadata on files.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags are simple labels attached to files:

vfs tag /report.pdf urgent
vfs tag /report.pdf quarterly
vfs find --tag urgent

docs.title: Custom Metadata
docs.text:
Key-value pairs for structured data:

vfs meta /report.pdf author "Jane Doe"
vfs meta /report.pdf department "Finance"
vfs meta /report.pdf status "approved"

docs.title: Metadata Use Cases
docs.text:
• Document Management: Author, status, review date
  • Asset Tracking: License, source, expiration
  • Workflow: Priority, assigned-to, due-date

docs.title: Storage Backends
docs.text:
VFS supports multiple database backends:

Backend Best For Trade-offs SQLite General use Excellent tooling, FTS5 search Sled High write throughput Pure Rust, modern LMDB Read-heavy workloads Memory-mapped, fast reads RocksDB Large datasets LSM-tree, SSD-optimized

The backend affects:

  • Performance characteristics
  • Search implementation (FTS5 vs Tantivy)
  • File size limits
  • Concurrency behavior

See Storage Backends for details.

docs.title: The Root Directory
docs.text:
Every vault has a root directory /. This is always your starting point.

# Root is always accessible
vfs ls /

# All paths are absolute from root
vfs cat /docs/readme.txt

# There is no "current directory" in VFS
# (except in interactive shell mode)

No Relative Paths

In normal CLI usage, all paths are absolute. The interactive shell supports cd and relative paths for convenience.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
Snapshots capture the entire vault state at a point in time.

# Save current state
vfs snapshot save before-refactor

# Make changes...
vfs rm -r /old-code
vfs mv /new-code /production

# Oops! Restore previous state
vfs snapshot restore before-refactor

Snapshots are useful for:

  • Experimentation: Try changes safely
  • Checkpoints: Save state before major operations
  • AI Agents: Provide rollback capability

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
VFS is designed around these core principles:

  1. Familiarity: Commands mirror standard Unix utilities
  2. Isolation: Virtual filesystems are completely separate from the host filesystem
  3. Portability: Each vault is a single database file
  4. Integrity: All operations are transactional - no partial writes
  5. Efficiency: Content-addressable storage for automatic deduplication
  6. Extensibility: Pluggable storage backends allow different database engines

docs.title: CLI Layer
docs.text: Parses command-line arguments using clap. Each command is a subcommand with its own argument structure. The interactive shell (vfs shell) provides a REPL that dispatches to the same command handlers.

docs.title: Command Layer
docs.text:
Business logic for each operation. Commands are stateless functions that receive parsed arguments and a storage interface. Each command:

  • Validates inputs
  • Performs the operation within a transaction
  • Returns results or errors

Commands are backend-agnostic - they interact only with the Storage Layer traits, never with database-specific APIs.

docs.title: Storage Layer
docs.text: The storage layer provides high-level abstractions over the raw database:

docs.title: PathResolver
docs.text:
• Resolves virtual paths to file IDs
  • Handles path normalization (/foo/../bar -> /bar)
  • Manages current working directory state
  • Validates path existence and permissions

docs.title: ContentStore
docs.text:
• Content-addressable storage using SHA-256 hashes
  • Deduplicates identical content across files
  • Handles BLOB storage and retrieval
  • Manages search indexes (backend-specific)

docs.title: VersionManager
docs.text:
• Creates new versions on every file modification
  • Stores version metadata (timestamp, size, hash)
  • Handles version retrieval and restoration
  • Implements pruning strategies

docs.title: Storage Backend Trait
docs.text:
The StorageBackend trait defines the interface that all database backends must implement:

pub trait StorageBackend: Send + Sync {
    /// Get a value by key
    fn get(&self, collection: &str, key: &[u8]) -> Result<Option<Vec<u8>>>;

    /// Store a value
    fn put(&self, collection: &str, key: &[u8], value: &[u8]) -> Result<()>;

    /// Delete a value
    fn delete(&self, collection: &str, key: &[u8]) -> Result<()>;

    /// Check if key exists
    fn exists(&self, collection: &str, key: &[u8]) -> Result<bool>;

    /// Scan keys with prefix
    fn scan_prefix(&self, collection: &str, prefix: &[u8])
        -> Result<Box<dyn Iterator<Item = (Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>)>>>;

    /// Execute operations atomically
    fn transaction<F, T>(&self, f: F) -> Result<T>
    where
        F: FnOnce(&dyn TransactionContext) -> Result<T>;

    /// Flush to disk
    fn sync(&self) -> Result<()>;

    /// Compact/optimize storage
    fn compact(&self) -> Result<()>;
}

pub trait SearchBackend: Send + Sync {
    /// Index content for full-text search
    fn index(&self, id: &str, content: &str) -> Result<()>;

    /// Remove from index
    fn unindex(&self, id: &str) -> Result<()>;

    /// Full-text search
    fn search(&self, query: &str, limit: usize) -> Result<Vec<SearchResult>>;
}

See Storage Backends for implementation details.

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text:
The storage layer uses these logical collections (mapped to tables/trees/buckets by backends):

Collection Key Value files file_id (u64) FileMetadata (serialized) paths path (string) file_id (u64) contents hash (SHA-256) blob data versions file_id + version_num VersionMetadata tags tag_name tag_id file_tags file_id + tag_id timestamp metadata file_id + key value settings key value

Data is serialized using a compact binary format (e.g., bincode, MessagePack, or CBOR).

docs.title: Vault Concept
docs.text:
A vault is an independent virtual filesystem stored in a single database file. Users can:

  • Create multiple vaults for different projects
  • Switch between vaults with vfs vault use
  • Back up vaults by copying the database file

Default vault location: ~/.vfs/vaults/

~/.vfs/
+-- config.toml          # Global configuration
+-- current_vault        # Tracks active vault
+-- vaults/
    +-- default.vfs      # SQLite backend (or .sled, .lmdb)
    +-- myproject.vfs
    +-- experiments.vfs

Vault files use the .vfs extension regardless of backend, with the backend type stored in metadata.

docs.title: Content-Addressable Storage
docs.text:
Files are stored using content-addressable storage (CAS):

  1. When a file is written, its content is hashed with SHA-256
  2. The content is stored in the contents collection keyed by hash
  3. The file entry references the content hash
  4. Multiple files with identical content share the same blob

Benefits:

  • Deduplication: Identical content stored once
  • Integrity: Hash verification catches corruption
  • Efficient versioning: Unchanged content isn't duplicated
files                          contents
+------------------------+     +------------------------------+
| path: /docs/readme.txt |---->| hash: abc123...              |
| content_hash: abc123...|     | data: "Hello, World!"        |
+------------------------+     | size: 13                     |
+------------------------+     | ref_count: 2                 |
| path: /backup/copy.txt |---->+------------------------------+
| content_hash: abc123...|
+------------------------+

docs.title: Transaction Safety
docs.text:
All storage backends must provide ACID transactions:

  • Atomic: Operations either complete fully or not at all
  • Consistent: Data integrity is maintained
  • Isolated: Concurrent operations don't interfere
  • Durable: Committed changes survive crashes

The transaction() method wraps multiple operations atomically.

docs.title: Search Architecture
docs.text:
Full-text search is handled by a separate SearchBackend trait:

Backend Search Implementation SQLite FTS5 extension (built-in) Sled/LMDB Tantivy (embedded Lucene-like engine) External Can integrate with MeiliSearch, Elasticsearch

The search index is kept in sync with content changes through the ContentStore.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Errors are propagated using Rust's Result type:

pub enum VfsError {
    NotFound(PathBuf),
    AlreadyExists(PathBuf),
    NotADirectory(PathBuf),
    NotAFile(PathBuf),
    InvalidPath(String),
    StorageError(Box<dyn std::error::Error>),
    SerializationError(String),
    IoError(std::io::Error),
}

Backend-specific errors are wrapped in StorageError to maintain abstraction.

docs.title: Adding a New Backend
docs.text:
To add a new storage backend:

  1. Implement StorageBackend trait
  2. Implement SearchBackend trait (or use tantivy adapter)
  3. Register in the backend factory
  4. Add CLI flag: --backend <name>

See Storage Backends for implementation guide.

docs.title: ls - List directory contents

vfs ls [OPTIONS] [PATH]

Options:

Option Description -l, --long Show detailed information (size, date, type) -a, --all Include hidden files (starting with .) -R, --recursive List subdirectories recursively -t, --time Sort by modification time -S, --size Sort by size

Examples:

vfs ls                    # List current directory
vfs ls /docs              # List specific directory
vfs ls -l /docs           # Detailed listing
vfs ls -laR /             # Full recursive listing

docs.text:
vfs grep [OPTIONS] <PATTERN> [PATH]...

docs.title: Database Schema
docs.text: This document describes the logical data model used by VFS. The model is backend-agnostic, with specific implementations for each storage backend.

docs.title: Logical Data Model
docs.text: VFS organizes data into collections (similar to tables or trees). Each collection stores key-value pairs with specific semantics.

docs.title: Collections Overview
docs.text: Collection Purpose Key Format Value Type files File/directory metadata file_id (u64) FileEntry paths Path to ID mapping path (string) file_id (u64) contents Content blobs (CAS) hash (32 bytes) ContentBlob versions Version history file_id + version_num VersionEntry tags Tag definitions tag_id (u64) TagInfo tag_names Tag name lookup tag_name (string) tag_id (u64) file_tags File-tag associations file_id + tag_id timestamp file_meta Custom metadata file_id + key value (string) settings Vault configuration key (string) value (string)

docs.title: FileEntry
docs.text:
Represents a file or directory in the virtual filesystem.

struct FileEntry {
    id: u64,
    parent_id: Option<u64>,     // None for root
    name: String,
    file_type: FileType,        // File or Directory
    content_hash: Option<Hash>, // None for directories
    size: u64,
    created_at: Timestamp,
    modified_at: Timestamp,
}

enum FileType {
    File,
    Directory,
}

Serialized format (bincode/MessagePack):

[id: 8 bytes][parent_id: 9 bytes][name: var][type: 1 byte]
[hash: 33 bytes][size: 8 bytes][created: 8 bytes][modified: 8 bytes]

docs.title: ContentBlob
docs.text:
Stores actual file content using content-addressable storage.

struct ContentBlob {
    hash: [u8; 32],      // SHA-256
    data: Vec<u8>,       // Raw content
    size: u64,
    ref_count: u32,      // Reference counting for GC
    created_at: Timestamp,
}

docs.title: VersionEntry
docs.text:
Records a point-in-time snapshot of a file.

struct VersionEntry {
    file_id: u64,
    version_num: u32,
    content_hash: Hash,
    size: u64,
    created_at: Timestamp,
}

Key format: file_id (8 bytes) + version_num (4 bytes)

docs.title: TagInfo
docs.text:
Defines a tag that can be applied to files.

struct TagInfo {
    id: u64,
    name: String,
    color: Option<String>,  // Hex color code
    created_at: Timestamp,
}

docs.title: Key Encoding
docs.text: Keys are encoded consistently across backends:

docs.title: Numeric Keys
docs.text:
• u64 values are encoded as big-endian bytes for proper ordering
  • Example: 1000 → [0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x03, 0xE8]

docs.title: String Keys
docs.text:
• UTF-8 encoded
  • Paths use forward slashes, no trailing slash (except root)

docs.title: Composite Keys
docs.text:
• Components are length-prefixed or use fixed sizes
  • Example file_tag key: file_id (8 bytes) + tag_id (8 bytes)
fn encode_file_tag_key(file_id: u64, tag_id: u64) -> [u8; 16] {
    let mut key = [0u8; 16];
    key[0..8].copy_from_slice(&file_id.to_be_bytes());
    key[8..16].copy_from_slice(&tag_id.to_be_bytes());
    key
}

docs.title: Value Serialization
docs.text: Values are serialized using a compact binary format:

docs.title: Primary: bincode
docs.text:
• Fast, compact, Rust-native
  • Used for internal structures

docs.title: Alternative: MessagePack
docs.text:
• More portable
  • Better for potential cross-language access

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[storage]
serialization = "bincode"  # or "msgpack", "cbor"

docs.title: SQLite Schema
docs.text:
When using SQLite, collections map to tables:

-- File metadata
CREATE TABLE files (
    id              INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    parent_id       INTEGER REFERENCES files(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    name            TEXT NOT NULL,
    file_type       INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- 0=file, 1=directory
    content_hash    BLOB,
    size            INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- Unix timestamp
    modified_at     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE(parent_id, name)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_files_parent ON files(parent_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_files_hash ON files(content_hash);

-- Path lookup (denormalized for performance)
CREATE TABLE paths (
    path    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    file_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES files(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- Content-addressable storage
CREATE TABLE contents (
    hash        BLOB PRIMARY KEY,  -- 32 bytes SHA-256
    data        BLOB NOT NULL,
    size        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    ref_count   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

-- Version history
CREATE TABLE versions (
    file_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    version_num INTEGER NOT NULL,
    content_hash BLOB NOT NULL,
    size        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    created_at  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_num)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_versions_created ON versions(created_at);

-- Tags
CREATE TABLE tags (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    color       TEXT,
    created_at  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE file_tags (
    file_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    tag_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    created_at  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, tag_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_file_tags_tag ON file_tags(tag_id);

-- Custom metadata
CREATE TABLE file_meta (
    file_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    key         TEXT NOT NULL,
    value       TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, key)
);

-- Full-text search (FTS5)
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE fts_content USING fts5(
    path,
    content,
    content_rowid='file_id'
);

-- Vault settings
CREATE TABLE settings (
    key     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    value   TEXT NOT NULL
);

docs.title: Sled/LMDB/RocksDB Schema
docs.text:
For key-value backends, collections map to separate trees/databases:

Tree: files
  Key: u64 (big-endian)
  Value: bincode(FileEntry)

Tree: paths
  Key: UTF-8 string
  Value: u64 (big-endian)

Tree: contents
  Key: 32 bytes (SHA-256)
  Value: raw bytes (content data)

Tree: contents_meta
  Key: 32 bytes (SHA-256)
  Value: bincode(ContentMeta { size, ref_count, created_at })

Tree: versions
  Key: file_id (8 bytes) + version_num (4 bytes)
  Value: bincode(VersionEntry)

Tree: tags
  Key: u64 (big-endian)
  Value: bincode(TagInfo)

Tree: tag_names
  Key: UTF-8 string
  Value: u64 (big-endian)

Tree: file_tags
  Key: file_id (8 bytes) + tag_id (8 bytes)
  Value: timestamp (8 bytes)

Tree: file_meta
  Key: file_id (8 bytes) + key_len (2 bytes) + key (UTF-8)
  Value: UTF-8 string

Tree: settings
  Key: UTF-8 string
  Value: UTF-8 string

Tree: _meta
  Key: "version" | "backend" | "created_at"
  Value: varies

Built-in full-text search:

-- Search
SELECT path, snippet(fts_content, 1, '<b>', '</b>', '...', 32) as snippet
FROM fts_content
WHERE fts_content MATCH ?
ORDER BY rank;

-- Index on insert
INSERT INTO fts_content(rowid, path, content)
VALUES (?, ?, ?);

INSERT INTO fts_content(rowid, path, content) VALUES (?, ?, ?);

Separate search index using tantivy:

let schema = Schema::builder()
    .add_text_field("path", TEXT | STORED)
    .add_text_field("content", TEXT)
    .add_u64_field("file_id", INDEXED | STORED)
    .build();

// Search

docs.title: Monotonic IDs (KV stores)
docs.text:
For key-value backends, use a counter in the settings collection:

fn next_id(storage: &dyn StorageBackend, collection: &str) -> Result<u64> {
    storage.transaction(|txn| {
        let key = format!("_next_id_{}", collection);
        let current: u64 = txn.get("settings", key.as_bytes())?
            .map(|v| u64::from_be_bytes(v.try_into().unwrap()))
            .unwrap_or(0);
        let next = current + 1;
        txn.put("settings", key.as_bytes(), &next.to_be_bytes())?;
        Ok(next)
    })
}

docs.text:
Remove unreferenced content blobs:

fn garbage_collect(storage: &dyn StorageBackend) -> Result<GcStats> {
    // 1. Scan contents_meta for ref_count = 0
    // 2. Delete from contents and contents_meta
}

docs.title: Version Pruning
docs.text:
Keep last N versions:

fn prune_versions(storage: &dyn StorageBackend, keep: u32) -> Result<PruneStats> {
    // For each file_id in versions:
    //   Get version count
    //   If > keep, delete oldest (version_num < max - keep)
    //   Decrement ref_count on deleted content hashes
}

SQLite:

DELETE FROM versions
WHERE (file_id, version_num) NOT IN (
    SELECT file_id, version_num FROM versions v2
    WHERE v2.file_id = versions.file_id
    ORDER BY version_num DESC
    LIMIT ?
);

docs.text:
Reclaim disk space:

Backend Method SQLite VACUUM Sled Automatic compaction LMDB Copy to new database RocksDB compact_range()

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
When migrating between backends, the migration tool:

  1. Opens source with old backend
  2. Creates destination with new backend
  3. Iterates all collections, copying key-value pairs
  4. Rebuilds search index
  5. Verifies integrity (checksums)

Data format (bincode) is the same across backends, so no transformation is needed.

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text: VFS provides familiar file operations that work just like their Unix counterparts.

docs.title: ls - List Directory Contents
docs.text:
vfs ls [OPTIONS] [PATH]

Options:

Option Description -l, --long Show detailed information (size, date, type) -a, --all Include hidden files (starting with .) -R, --recursive List subdirectories recursively -t, --time Sort by modification time -S, --size Sort by size

Examples:

vfs ls                    # List current directory
vfs ls /docs              # List specific directory
vfs ls -l /docs           # Detailed listing
vfs ls -laR /             # Full recursive listing

docs.title: tree - Display Directory Tree
docs.text:
vfs tree [OPTIONS] [PATH]

Options:

Option Description -L, --level <N> Limit depth to N levels -d, --dirs-only Show only directories --size Show file sizes

Examples:

vfs tree                  # Tree from root
vfs tree -L 2 /           # Tree with max depth 2
vfs tree --size /docs     # Tree with file sizes

docs.title: pwd - Print Working Directory
docs.text:
vfs pwd

In VFS, the working directory is always / unless you're in the interactive shell.

docs.title: cat - Display File Contents
docs.text:
vfs cat [OPTIONS] <PATH>...

Options:

Option Description -n, --number Number output lines -v, --version <N> Show specific version

Examples:

vfs cat /docs/readme.txt          # Show file contents
vfs cat -n /src/main.rs           # With line numbers
vfs cat -v 3 /docs/readme.txt     # Show version 3
vfs cat file1.txt file2.txt       # Concatenate multiple files

docs.title: write - Write Content to a File
docs.text:
vfs write [OPTIONS] <PATH> [CONTENT]

Options:

Option Description -a, --append Append instead of overwrite --stdin Read content from stdin

Examples:

# Write content directly
vfs write /docs/new.txt "Hello, World!"

# Append to existing file
vfs write -a /docs/log.txt "New line"

# From stdin
echo "piped content" | vfs write --stdin /docs/file.txt

# Multi-line content
vfs write /docs/multi.txt "Line 1
Line 2
Line 3"

Version Created

Every write operation creates a new version of the file, enabling rollback.

docs.title: cp - Copy Files or Directories
docs.text:
vfs cp [OPTIONS] <SOURCE>... <DEST>

Options:

Option Description -r, --recursive Copy directories recursively -f, --force Overwrite without prompting -n, --no-clobber Don't overwrite existing files

Examples:

# Copy a file
vfs cp /docs/readme.txt /docs/backup.txt

# Copy multiple files to a directory
vfs cp /src/a.txt /src/b.txt /backup/

# Copy directory recursively
vfs cp -r /docs /docs-backup

# Copy with rename
vfs cp /config.txt /config.txt.bak

docs.title: mv - Move or Rename Files
docs.text:
vfs mv [OPTIONS] <SOURCE>... <DEST>

Options:

Option Description -f, --force Overwrite without prompting -n, --no-clobber Don't overwrite existing files

Examples:

# Rename a file
vfs mv /docs/old.txt /docs/new.txt

# Move file to directory
vfs mv /readme.txt /docs/

# Move multiple files
vfs mv /file1.txt /file2.txt /archive/

# Move and rename
vfs mv /src/main.rs /backup/main.rs.bak

docs.title: mkdir - Create Directories
docs.text:
vfs mkdir [OPTIONS] <PATH>...

Options:

Option Description -p, --parents Create parent directories as needed

Examples:

# Create a directory
vfs mkdir /docs

# Create nested directories
vfs mkdir -p /src/components/ui

# Create multiple directories
vfs mkdir /logs /temp /cache

docs.title: rm - Remove Files or Directories
docs.text:
vfs rm [OPTIONS] <PATH>...

Options:

Option Description -r, --recursive Remove directories and their contents -f, --force Don't prompt for confirmation

Examples:

# Remove a file
vfs rm /docs/old.txt

# Remove multiple files
vfs rm /temp/a.txt /temp/b.txt

# Remove empty directory
vfs rm /empty-dir

# Remove directory with contents
vfs rm -r /old-project

# Force remove without confirmation
vfs rm -rf /temp/

Permanent Deletion

Removed files are deleted from the filesystem. However, content may still exist in the blob store until garbage collection runs. Use versioning to recover recent files before they're pruned.

docs.title: Import & Export
docs.text: VFS provides commands to bridge between the virtual filesystem and the real filesystem, plus the ability to run external commands on virtual files.

docs.title: Import Files
docs.text: Import files from the real filesystem into a vault.

docs.title: Basic Import
docs.text:
vfs import <real_path> <vfs_path>

Examples:

# Import a single file
vfs import ~/documents/report.pdf /docs/report.pdf

# Import to current directory
vfs import ~/data.csv /data.csv

# Import with different name
vfs import ~/old-name.txt /new-name.txt

docs.title: Recursive Import
docs.text:
Import entire directories:

vfs import -r ~/project /project

Options:

Option Description -r, --recursive Import directories recursively --max-depth <N> Limit recursion depth

Examples:

# Import directory tree
vfs import -r ~/src /src

# Limit depth
vfs import -r --max-depth 2 ~/project /project

docs.title: Export Files
docs.text: Export files from a vault to the real filesystem.

docs.title: Basic Export
docs.text:
vfs export <vfs_path> <real_path>

Examples:

# Export a single file
vfs export /docs/report.pdf ~/downloads/report.pdf

# Export to current directory
vfs export /config.yaml ./config.yaml

docs.title: Recursive Export
docs.text:
Export entire directories:

vfs export -r /project ~/exported-project

Options:

Option Description -r, --recursive Export directories recursively --max-depth <N> Limit recursion depth --overwrite Overwrite existing files

Examples:

# Export with overwrite
vfs export -r --overwrite /backup ~/backup

# Export specific version
vfs export --version 3 /docs/readme.txt ~/old-readme.txt

docs.title: External Commands (exec)
docs.text: Run external bash commands on virtual files.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. File is extracted to a secure temp directory
  2. Command runs with the temp file
  3. Modified file is re-imported (creating a new version)
  4. Temp file is deleted

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
vfs exec '<COMMAND>' <PATH>

Examples:

# In-place text replacement with sed
vfs exec 'sed -i s/foo/bar/g' /docs/file.txt

# Format JSON with jq
vfs exec 'jq .' /config/settings.json

# Sort lines in a file
vfs exec 'sort -o {} {}' /data/names.txt

The {} placeholder is replaced with the temp file path.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --reimport Re-import the modified file (default) --stdin Pass file content via stdin

docs.title: No Re-import
docs.text:
Run command without modifying the virtual file:

# Just view the output
vfs exec 'wc -l' /data/file.txt

docs.title: Pipe-Based Operations
docs.text: For streaming data, use pipes with cat and write:

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: vfs cat <PATH> | <command> | vfs write <PATH>

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Sort and deduplicate
vfs cat /data/names.txt | sort | uniq | vfs write /data/names-sorted.txt

# Filter log lines
vfs cat /logs/app.log | grep ERROR | vfs write /logs/errors.log

# Transform JSON
vfs cat /config/settings.json | jq '.debug = true' | vfs write /config/settings.json

# Compress content
vfs cat /data/large.txt | gzip | vfs write /data/large.txt.gz

docs.title: Reading from External Sources
docs.text:
# Pipe from real filesystem
cat ~/real-file.txt | vfs write /imported/file.txt

# Pipe from curl
curl -s https://api.example.com/data | vfs write /api/response.json

# Pipe from any command
date | vfs write /logs/timestamp.txt

docs.title: Writing to External Destinations
docs.text:
# View in pager
vfs cat /docs/readme.txt | less

# Send to clipboard (Linux)
vfs cat /notes/snippet.txt | xclip -selection clipboard

# Convert with pandoc
vfs cat /report.md | pandoc -t pdf > report.pdf

docs.title: exec vs Pipe Comparison
docs.text: Feature vfs exec Pipe In-place editing Yes Yes Multiple files With globs One at a time Temp file created Yes No Streaming support No Yes Large files Memory-limited Stream-friendly

docs.title: When to Use exec
docs.text:
• Commands that require file paths (not stdin/stdout)
  • Commands that modify files in-place (like sed -i)
  • When you need automatic versioning on modification

docs.title: When to Use Pipes
docs.text:
• Streaming large files
  • Complex multi-stage pipelines
  • Commands designed for stdin/stdout

docs.title: Backup to Real Filesystem
docs.text:
# Export entire vault
vfs export -r / ~/vault-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

docs.title: Import Project Files
docs.text:
# Import a project
vfs import -r ~/code/myproject /myproject

# Verify
vfs tree /myproject

docs.title: Process Files with External Tools
docs.text:
# Format all JSON files
for file in $(vfs find / -n "*.json"); do
    vfs exec 'jq .' "$file"
done

# Or using cat/write for complex pipelines
vfs cat /data.csv | \
    cut -d',' -f1,3 | \
    sort -t',' -k2 | \
    head -100 | \
    vfs write /data-processed.csv

docs.title: Metadata & Tags
docs.text: VFS supports rich metadata for organizing and finding files through tags and custom key-value attributes.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags are labels you can attach to files for organization and quick retrieval.

docs.title: Adding Tags
docs.text:
vfs tag <path> <tag>...

Examples:

# Single tag
vfs tag /docs/report.pdf important

# Multiple tags
vfs tag /docs/report.pdf important urgent work

docs.title: Tags on a file
docs.text:
$ vfs tag /docs/report.pdf --list
important, urgent, work

docs.title: All tags in vault
docs.text:
$ vfs tag --list-all
TAG          COUNT
important    23
urgent       8
work         156
personal     45
code         234

docs.title: Removing Tags
docs.text:
vfs untag <path> <tag>

Examples:

# Remove single tag
vfs untag /docs/report.pdf urgent

# Remove from pattern
vfs untag /archive/*.txt important

docs.title: Finding Files by Tag
docs.text:
vfs find / --tag <tag>

Examples:

$ vfs find / --tag important
/docs/report.pdf
/config/production.yaml
/notes/meeting-2024-03-10.md

# Multiple tags (AND)
$ vfs find / --tag important --tag urgent
/docs/report.pdf

docs.title: Managing Tags
docs.text:
# Create a new tag
vfs tag --create important

# Rename a tag
vfs tag --rename old-tag new-tag

# Delete a tag (removes from all files)
vfs tag --delete unused-tag

docs.title: Custom Metadata
docs.text: Beyond tags, you can store arbitrary key-value metadata on files.

docs.title: Setting Metadata
docs.text:
vfs meta <path> <key> <value>

Examples:

# Set author
vfs meta /docs/report.pdf author "Jane Doe"

# Set multiple properties
vfs meta /docs/report.pdf department "Engineering"
vfs meta /docs/report.pdf status "draft"
vfs meta /docs/report.pdf priority "high"

# Numeric values
vfs meta /data/dataset.csv row_count "10000"

# Date values
vfs meta /docs/contract.pdf signed_date "2024-03-15"

docs.title: Reading Metadata
docs.text:
# Get specific key
$ vfs meta /docs/report.pdf author
Jane Doe

# Get all metadata
$ vfs meta /docs/report.pdf
KEY          VALUE
author       Jane Doe
department   Engineering
status       draft
priority     high

docs.title: Removing Metadata
docs.text: vfs meta /docs/report.pdf --delete status

docs.title: Finding by Metadata
docs.text:
vfs find / --meta <key>=<value>

Examples:

# Find by author
$ vfs find / --meta author="Jane Doe"
/docs/report.pdf
/docs/presentation.pdf

# Find by status
$ vfs find / --meta status=draft
/docs/report.pdf
/src/feature.rs

docs.title: Export/Import Metadata
docs.text:
# Export metadata to JSON
vfs meta /docs/ --export > metadata.json

# Import metadata from JSON
vfs meta --import metadata.json

JSON format:

{
  "/docs/report.pdf": {
    "tags": ["important", "work"],
    "metadata": {
      "author": "Jane Doe",
      "status": "draft"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Project Organization
docs.text:
# Set up project tags
vfs tag --create frontend
vfs tag --create backend
vfs tag --create docs

# Tag project files
vfs tag /src/ui/*.tsx frontend
vfs tag /src/api/*.rs backend
vfs tag /docs/*.md docs

# Find all frontend code
vfs find / --tag frontend

docs.title: Document Management
docs.text:
# Track document metadata
vfs meta /contracts/client-a.pdf client "Acme Corp"
vfs meta /contracts/client-a.pdf value "50000"
vfs meta /contracts/client-a.pdf expires "2025-12-31"

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
# Organize research
vfs tag /notes/paper-1.md read cite
vfs meta /notes/paper-1.md source "arxiv:2024.12345"
vfs meta /notes/paper-1.md relevance "high"

# Find papers to cite
vfs find /notes --tag cite

docs.title: Search
docs.text: VFS provides powerful search capabilities for finding files by name, content, and attributes.

docs.title: Full-Text Search
docs.text: VFS uses SQLite FTS5 for fast full-text search across all file contents.

docs.title: Basic Search
docs.text:
vfs search <query>

Examples:

$ vfs search "database connection"
/src/db.rs:15: let connection = Database::connect(url)?;
/docs/setup.md:42: Configure your database connection string...
/config/example.yaml:8: database_connection: postgres://...

$ vfs search "TODO"
/src/main.rs:23: // TODO: implement error handling
/src/lib.rs:89: // TODO: add tests

docs.title: Search in Directory
docs.text: vfs search "query" /path/

docs.title: Search Options
docs.text: Option Description --limit <N> Limit results --rebuild Rebuild search index --json JSON output

docs.title: FTS5 Query Syntax
docs.text:
VFS supports SQLite FTS5 query syntax for advanced searches:

# Phrase search
vfs search '"exact phrase"'

# AND (default)
vfs search "database connection"  # finds both words

# OR
vfs search "error OR warning"

# NOT
vfs search "config NOT test"

# Prefix matching
vfs search "data*"  # matches database, datatype, etc.

docs.title: Grep - Regex Search
docs.text: The grep command provides regex-based searching with more control.

docs.title: Basic Grep
docs.text:
vfs grep <pattern> [path]

Examples:

$ vfs grep "fn \w+\(" /src/
/src/main.rs:5:fn main() {
/src/main.rs:12:fn process_args(args: &[String]) -> Result<Config> {
/src/lib.rs:8:fn new() -> Self {

docs.title: Regex Patterns
docs.text:
VFS uses Rust's regex crate:

# Character classes
vfs grep "[0-9]+" /data/          # Numbers
vfs grep "[A-Z][a-z]+" /docs/     # Capitalized words

# Quantifiers
vfs grep "colou?r" /docs/         # color or colour

# Anchors
vfs grep "^import" /src/          # Lines starting with import
vfs grep ";\s*$" /src/            # Lines ending with semicolon

# Groups
vfs grep "(TODO|FIXME|HACK)" /src/

docs.title: Grep Options
docs.text: Option Description -i, --ignore-case Case-insensitive -n, --line-numbers Show line numbers (default) -l, --files-with-matches Only show filenames -c, --count Show match count --limit <N> Limit results

docs.title: Context Lines
docs.text:
# 3 lines after each match
$ vfs grep -A 3 "fn main" /src/main.rs
/src/main.rs:5:fn main() {
/src/main.rs-6-    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().collect();
/src/main.rs-7-    let config = process_args(&args)?;

# 2 lines before and after
vfs grep -C 2 "error" /logs/app.log

docs.title: Find - Locate Files
docs.text: The find command locates files by name, attributes, and metadata.

docs.title: Find by Name
docs.text:
vfs find [path] -n <pattern>

Uses glob patterns:

# All text files
vfs find / -n "*.txt"

# Files starting with "test"
vfs find /src -n "test*"

# Single character wildcard
vfs find / -n "file?.txt"  # file1.txt, fileA.txt, etc.

docs.title: Find by Type
docs.text:
# Files only
vfs find / -t f

# Directories only
vfs find / -t d

docs.title: Find by Size
docs.text:
# Files larger than 10MB
vfs find / --min-size 10485760

# Files smaller than 1KB
vfs find / --max-size 1024

docs.title: Find by Tag
docs.text:
vfs find / --tag important
vfs find / --tag work --tag urgent  # Multiple tags

docs.title: Find by Metadata
docs.text: vfs find / --meta author="Jane Doe"

docs.title: Combining Conditions
docs.text:
# Large Rust files
vfs find /src -n "*.rs" --min-size 10240

# Files with specific tag
vfs find /docs --tag important

docs.title: Rebuild Index
docs.text:
If search seems slow or incomplete:

vfs search --rebuild

docs.title: Search Large Vaults
docs.text:
For very large vaults:

# Limit results
vfs search --limit 100 "pattern"

# Search specific directory
vfs search "pattern" /relevant/directory/

# Use grep for targeted search
vfs grep "pattern" /specific/file.txt

docs.title: Standard Output
docs.text:
$ vfs grep "error" /logs/
/logs/app.log:15:Error: Connection failed
/logs/app.log:23:error handling exception

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
$ vfs grep --json "error" /logs/
{
  "matches": [
    {
      "path": "/logs/app.log",
      "line": 15,
      "content": "Error: Connection failed"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Find and Process
docs.text:
# Find all Python files
vfs find /src -n "*.py" | while read file; do
    echo "Processing $file"
    vfs cat "$file" | wc -l
done

docs.title: Search with Tags
docs.text:
# Search only in tagged files
vfs find / --tag code | while read file; do
    vfs grep "TODO" "$file"
done

docs.title: Export Search Results
docs.text:
# Create report of all TODOs
vfs grep "TODO|FIXME" /src/ > ~/todos-report.txt

docs.title: Interactive Shell
docs.text: VFS provides an interactive shell mode where you can use commands without the vfs prefix.

docs.title: Starting the Shell
docs.text:
vfs shell

This launches an interactive REPL:

$ vfs shell
vfs - Virtual Filesystem Shell
Type 'help' for commands, 'exit' to quit.

[default] / >

docs.title: Prompt Format
docs.text:
The prompt shows:

  • Vault name: Current active vault
  • Current path: Working directory within the vault
[vault-name] /current/path >

Examples:

[default] / >
[myproject] /src >
[backup] /documents/2024 >

docs.title: Using Commands
docs.text:
In shell mode, commands work without the vfs prefix:

[default] / > ls
docs/
src/
config/

[default] / > cd docs

[default] /docs > cat readme.txt
Welcome to the project!

[default] /docs > mkdir archive

[default] /docs > cp readme.txt archive/

[default] /docs > ls archive/
readme.txt

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text: All VFS commands work in the shell:

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Command Description ls [path] List directory contents cd [path] Change directory pwd Print working directory tree [path] Display directory tree

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text: Command Description cat <file> Display file contents write <file> text Write text to file cp <src> <dst> Copy files mv <src> <dst> Move/rename files rm <path> Remove files mkdir <dir> Create directory

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Command Description grep <pat> [path] Search file contents find [path] [opt] Find files search <query> Full-text search

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Command Description log <file> Show version history checkout <f> -v <v> Restore version revert <file> Revert to previous diff <f1> <f2> Compare files

docs.title: Vault
docs.text: Command Description vault list List vaults vault use <name> Switch vault vault info Vault information

docs.title: Shell
docs.text: Command Description help Show help exit Exit shell (or Ctrl+D) clear Clear screen

docs.title: Tab Completion
docs.text: The shell supports tab completion for:

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
[default] / > gr<TAB>
grep

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
[default] / > cd do<TAB>
[default] / > cd docs/

[default] /docs > cat re<TAB>
[default] /docs > cat readme.txt

docs.title: Navigate History
docs.text:
• Up Arrow: Previous command
  • Down Arrow: Next command
  • Ctrl+R: Reverse search history

docs.title: History Persistence
docs.text:
Command history is saved to ~/.vfs/history and persists across sessions.

Disable history with:

vfs shell --no-history

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl+A Move to start of line Ctrl+E Move to end of line Ctrl+U Clear line before cursor Ctrl+K Clear line after cursor Ctrl+W Delete word before cursor Ctrl+L Clear screen Ctrl+C Cancel current command Ctrl+D Exit shell (if line empty) Tab Auto-complete

docs.title: Shell Aliases
docs.text:
Generate aliases for your regular shell:

$ vfs aliases
alias vls='vfs ls'
alias vcat='vfs cat'
alias vwrite='vfs write'
...

docs.title: Add to Shell Configuration
docs.text:
BashZshFish 
# Add to ~/.bashrc
eval "$(vfs aliases --format bash)"

# Add to ~/.zshrc
eval "$(vfs aliases --format zsh)"

# Add to ~/.config/fish/config.fish
vfs aliases --format fish | source

Then use directly from your shell:

$ vls /docs
$ vcat /docs/readme.txt

docs.title: Quick Directory Navigation
docs.text:
# Go to root
cd /

# Go up one level
cd ..

# Go to specific path
cd /src/components

docs.title: Use Relative Paths
docs.text:
In the shell, relative paths work:

[default] /docs > cat ./readme.txt
[default] /docs > ls ../src/

docs.title: Switch Vaults Quickly
docs.text:
[default] / > vault use myproject
[myproject] / > vault use default
[default] / >

docs.title: Vault Management
docs.text: A vault is an independent virtual filesystem stored in a single database file (.vfs extension). VFS supports multiple vaults, allowing you to organize different projects, experiments, or backups in isolated containers.

docs.title: What is a Vault?
docs.text:
• A complete virtual filesystem in one .vfs file
  • Contains files, directories, versions, tags, and metadata
  • Fully isolated from other vaults
  • Portable - copy the file to move your filesystem

docs.title: Default Storage Location
docs.text:
~/.vfs/
├── config.toml          # Global vfs configuration
├── current              # Name of the active vault
└── vaults/
    ├── default.vfs       # The default vault
    ├── myproject.vfs     # User-created vault
    └── experiments.vfs   # Another vault

docs.title: Basic Creation
docs.text:
vfs vault create <name>

Creates a new vault in the default location (~/.vfs/vaults/<name>.vfs).

$ vfs vault create myproject
Created vault 'myproject' at ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs
Switched to vault 'myproject'

docs.title: Custom Location
docs.text:
Store the vault database at a custom location:

# External drive
vfs vault create backup --path /mnt/external/backup.vfs

# Project directory
vfs vault create project-files --path ./project.vfs

docs.title: Listing Vaults
docs.text:
$ vfs vault list
  VAULT          SIZE      FILES    VERSIONS   PATH
* default        12.3 MB   234      1,892      ~/.vfs/vaults/default.vfs
  myproject      4.5 MB    89       456        ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs
  experiments    128 KB    12       24         ~/.vfs/vaults/experiments.vfs

* = active vault

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text: vfs vault list --json

docs.title: Switching Vaults
docs.text:
vfs vault use <name>

Switch to a different vault:

$ vfs vault use myproject
Switched to vault 'myproject'

docs.title: Temporary Vault Override
docs.text:
Use --vault flag with any command to temporarily use a different vault:

# List files in another vault without switching
vfs --vault backup ls /documents

# Copy between vaults
vfs cat /file.txt | vfs --vault backup write /file.txt

docs.title: Vault Information
docs.text:
vfs vault info [name]

Show detailed information about a vault:

$ vfs vault info myproject
Vault: myproject
Path: ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs
Size: 4.5 MB

Statistics:
  Files: 89
  Directories: 23
  Total versions: 456
  Content blobs: 312

Created: 2024-01-15 10:30:00
Last modified: 2024-03-10 14:22:15

docs.title: Deleting Vaults
docs.text:
vfs vault delete <name>

Delete a vault permanently:

$ vfs vault delete experiments
This will permanently delete vault 'experiments' and all its contents.
Are you sure? [y/N] y
Deleted vault 'experiments'

docs.title: Force Delete
docs.text:
Skip confirmation prompt:

vfs vault delete experiments --force

Cannot Delete Active Vault

You cannot delete the currently active vault. Switch to another vault first.

docs.title: Backup a Vault
docs.text:
Since a vault is a single SQLite file, backup is simple:

# Copy the database file
cp ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs ~/backups/myproject-$(date +%Y%m%d).vfs

docs.title: Online Backup
docs.text:
For backing up while VFS is in use:

sqlite3 ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs ".backup ~/backups/myproject.vfs"

docs.title: Restore from Backup
docs.text:
# Copy backup to vaults directory
cp ~/backups/myproject-backup.vfs ~/.vfs/vaults/restored.vfs
vfs vault use restored

docs.title: Moving Vaults Between Machines
docs.text:
1. Copy the .vfs file to the target machine
  2. Place it in ~/.vfs/vaults/ or use a custom path
# On source machine
scp ~/.vfs/vaults/myproject.vfs user@target:~/.vfs/vaults/

# On target machine
vfs vault use myproject

docs.title: Cloud Sync
docs.text:
Vault files can be synced via cloud storage:

# Store vault in Dropbox
vfs vault create shared --path ~/Dropbox/vfs/shared.vfs

Concurrent Access

SQLite databases shouldn't be accessed concurrently from multiple machines. Use proper locking or sync only when not in use.

docs.title: Vault Locked
docs.text:
Error: Vault is locked by another process

Another VFS instance is using the vault. Check for:

  • Other terminal sessions
  • Background VFS processes
  • Stale lock files

docs.title: Corrupt Vault
docs.text:
If a vault becomes corrupted:

# Check integrity
sqlite3 ~/.vfs/vaults/damaged.vfs "PRAGMA integrity_check"

# Attempt recovery
sqlite3 ~/.vfs/vaults/damaged.vfs ".recover" | sqlite3 recovered.vfs

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: VFS automatically tracks version history for all files. Every time a file is modified, a new version is created, allowing you to view history, compare changes, and restore previous versions.

docs.title: Automatic Versioning
docs.text:
Unlike traditional version control systems, VFS doesn't require explicit commits:

  • Every write operation creates a new version
  • No manual commits needed
  • Instant rollback to any previous state
  • Zero-effort history for all files

docs.title: When Versions Are Created
docs.text: Operation Creates Version? vfs write Yes vfs cp (overwrite) Yes vfs mv (overwrite) Yes vfs exec (modifies file) Yes Pipe write Yes vfs rm No (file deleted)

docs.title: File Version Log
docs.text:
vfs log <path>

Shows version history for a file:

$ vfs log /docs/readme.txt
VERSION  SIZE     DATE                 HASH (first 8)
7        1.2 KB   2024-03-10 14:22:15  a1b2c3d4
6        1.1 KB   2024-03-09 10:15:00  e5f6g7h8
5        1.0 KB   2024-03-08 09:30:22  i9j0k1l2
4        980 B    2024-03-07 16:45:11  m3n4o5p6
3        850 B    2024-03-05 11:20:00  q7r8s9t0
2        500 B    2024-03-01 09:00:00  u1v2w3x4
1        128 B    2024-02-28 15:30:00  y5z6a7b8

docs.title: Limit History
docs.text: vfs log -n 5 /docs/readme.txt    # Last 5 versions only

docs.title: Cat with Version
docs.text:
vfs cat -v <version> <path>

Read a specific version:

$ vfs cat -v 3 /docs/readme.txt
# This shows the content from version 3

docs.title: Export Past Version
docs.text: vfs export --version 3 /docs/readme.txt ~/old-readme.txt

docs.title: Diff Current vs Past
docs.text:
vfs diff --v1 <version> <path>

Compare current version with a past version:

$ vfs diff --v1 5 /docs/readme.txt
--- /docs/readme.txt (version 5)
+++ /docs/readme.txt (current)
@@ -1,4 +1,6 @@
 # README

-This is the old content.
+This is the updated content.
+With new lines added.

docs.title: Diff Two Past Versions
docs.text:
vfs diff --v1 3 --v2 5 /docs/readme.txt

Compare version 3 to version 5.

docs.title: Checkout
docs.text:
vfs checkout <path> -v <version>

Restore a file to a specific version. This creates a new version (non-destructive):

$ vfs checkout /docs/readme.txt -v 3
Restored /docs/readme.txt to version 3
(created as version 8)

$ vfs log -n 2 /docs/readme.txt
VERSION  SIZE     DATE                 HASH
8        850 B    2024-03-10 15:00:00  q7r8s9t0  # Same content as v3
7        1.2 KB   2024-03-10 14:22:15  a1b2c3d4

docs.title: Revert
docs.text:
vfs revert <path>

Shortcut to restore the immediately previous version:

$ vfs revert /docs/readme.txt
Reverted /docs/readme.txt from version 7 to version 6
(created as version 8)

docs.title: How Versions Work
docs.text:
VFS uses content-addressable storage:

  1. File content is hashed (SHA-256)
  2. Content is stored in blob table
  3. Version metadata points to the content hash
  4. Identical content is stored only once
Version 1: hash → abc123 (points to content "Hello")
Version 2: hash → def456 (points to content "Hello World")
Version 3: hash → abc123 (same as v1, no extra storage)

docs.title: Storage Efficiency
docs.text:
• Unchanged content isn't duplicated
  • Only actual changes consume space
  • Reference counting tracks content usage

docs.title: Directory Versioning
docs.text: Directories themselves don't have versions, but you can track changes across a directory:

docs.title: Log for Directory
docs.text:
vfs log /docs/

Shows recent versions across all files in the directory:

$ vfs log /docs/
PATH                    VERSION  DATE
/docs/readme.txt        7        2024-03-10 14:22:15
/docs/guide.md          3        2024-03-10 12:00:00
/docs/api.txt           12       2024-03-09 16:30:00

docs.title: Pruning Old Versions
docs.text:
To manage storage, you can prune old versions. See Maintenance for details.

Quick overview:

# Keep only last 5 versions per file
vfs prune --keep 5

# Remove versions older than 30 days
vfs prune --older-than 30

# Preview what would be removed
vfs prune --keep 5 --dry-run

docs.title: Use Tags for Milestones
docs.text:
Mark important versions with metadata:

# Make changes
vfs write /config/app.yaml "..."

docs.title: Export Before Major Changes
docs.text:
Before risky operations:

vfs export /important/file.txt ~/backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).txt

docs.title: Regular Pruning
docs.text:
Set up regular pruning to manage storage:

# Run pruning
vfs prune --keep 10

# Or run full maintenance
vfs maintain

docs.title: "Version not found"
docs.text:
The version may have been pruned. Check available versions:

vfs log /path/to/file

docs.title: Large Version Count
docs.text:
If a file has too many versions:

# Check version count
vfs log /file | wc -l

# Prune aggressively
vfs prune --keep 10 /file
